title: M1 Alternatives 2026: Fees, Cash Rates and Features Compared
h1: M1 Alternatives 2026: Fees, Features and Limits Compared
metaDescription: M1 alternatives compared: Betterment, Wealthfront, Fidelity, Robinhood, Public, Acorns and Webull by published fees, cash rates and margin costs.
intro:
Betterment, Wealthfront, Fidelity, Robinhood, Public, Acorns and Webull are the seven primary alternatives to [M1](https://www.m1.com). The differences sit in how each charges (a flat platform fee, an advisory percentage, a monthly subscription or zero trading commissions), whether the investor designs the portfolio or the provider selects it, cash interest and margin borrowing rates.

M1 describes itself as an Artificial Intelligence (AI) wealth management platform combining investing, saving and borrowing in one place. It serves over 400,000 clients with more than $14 billion in client assets as of September 2026. Self-directed brokerage accounts carry no commission, trading or management fees, but M1 applies a $3 monthly platform fee that is waived for clients holding more than $10,000 across accounts. M1 is built for long-term investors and states plainly that it is not a day-trading platform, using once or twice daily trade windows rather than continuous order execution.

For readers who want managed portfolios instead of picking individual holdings, our [best robo-advisors roundup](/roundup/best-robo-advisors/) covers automated investing options. If you are starting your first taxable account, see the [best investment apps for beginners](/roundup/best-investment-apps-for-beginners/). For tax-advantaged retirement saving, browse the [best IRA accounts](/roundup/best-ira-accounts/). You can also review our [Betterment alternatives](/alternatives/betterment/), [Wealthfront alternatives](/alternatives/wealthfront/), [Robinhood alternatives](/alternatives/robinhood/), [Acorns alternatives](/alternatives/acorns/) and [Fidelity alternatives](/alternatives/fidelity/) guides, or browse every side-by-side review in our [comparison hub](/compare/).

chooseSection.heading: How to Choose an M1 Alternative
chooseSection.body:
Selecting an alternative to M1 begins with how your portfolio is constructed and who manages the individual holdings. M1 lets you build custom investment allocations called Pies using stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), or accept guidance from M1 Advisor. Fractional shares allow you to set exact percentage targets for each slice of the Pie. If you prefer to have a provider select the portfolio for you, Betterment, Wealthfront and Fidelity Go function as robo-advisors. If you prefer to trade individual stocks and options continuously throughout the trading day, Fidelity, Robinhood, Public and Webull provide real-time order execution.

Second, evaluate trading mechanics and scheduling constraints. M1 does not support day trading, extended-hours trading, limit orders, short selling, options, futures, mutual funds or over-the-counter (OTC) stocks. All orders execute in scheduled windows once or twice per day. In contrast, Robinhood, Webull and Fidelity offer self-directed trading for stocks, ETFs and options with no commissions. If you require immediate execution at a specific limit price, an alternative with continuous market trading is required.

Third, calculate the ongoing software and subscription costs based on your balance size. M1 charges a $3 monthly platform fee, which equals $36 per year. That fee is waived if your total assets on M1 exceed $10,000. Betterment charges $5 per month ($60 per year) on balances under $24,000 unless you schedule a recurring monthly deposit of at least $200, which switches the pricing to a 0.25% annual fee. Wealthfront charges a straight 0.25% annual advisory fee on The Wealthfront Portfolio with no subscription, while its self-directed brokerage account costs $0. Acorns uses a subscription model costing $4, $8 or $12 per month ($48, $96 or $144 annually). Fidelity charges $0 for self-directed brokerage and $0 on Fidelity Go for accounts holding under $25,000.

Fourth, compare cash interest rates and margin borrowing expenses. M1 pays a 3.35% Annual Percentage Yield (APY) on its High-Yield Cash Account, requiring an initial deposit of $100, and offers margin borrowing at 5.90% for brokerage accounts with at least $2,000 in eligible securities. Public lists a High-Yield Cash Account at 3.30% APY (and 3.75% in promotional copy) alongside a 5.15% base margin rate. Robinhood Gold lists 3.6% APY on cash for $5 per month, while Wealthfront pays a 3.55% base cash APY with no monthly account fee. Fidelity lists a higher effective margin rate of 12.075% on balances under $25,000 based on its 10.825% base rate.

Check these five factors before selecting an alternative:

- Do you want to build custom fractional-share percentage targets or have a provider manage the portfolio?
- Do you need continuous real-time market execution, or do daily batch windows fit your goals?
- Does your balance clear M1's $10,000 threshold to waive its $3 monthly fee, or would a zero-fee broker cost less?
- What interest rate does your uninvested cash earn, and what deposit is required?
- If you plan to borrow on margin, what is the published borrowing rate for your portfolio size?

alternatives.heading: Betterment
alternatives.body:
Betterment provides automated portfolio management alongside a self-directed investing option with zero commissions. For automated investing, Betterment charges $5 per month for account balances between $0 and $24,000. That flat charge switches to an annual fee of 0.25% when an investor maintains a recurring monthly deposit of $200 or more, or once the total investing balance reaches $24,000. Assets between $1 million and $2 million pay a discounted 0.15% fee, and assets above $2 million pay 0.10% on that portion. Betterment Premium charges 0.65% annually on the first $1 million, requires a $100,000 minimum eligible investment balance, and provides access to financial experts. The Cash Reserve account charges no monthly management fees, requires a $10 minimum deposit for the base rate, and lists a 3.50% variable APY as of September 21, 2026, with an optional 0.75% boost for qualifying new clients.

Betterment fits hands-off investors who want automated portfolios selected by the provider, with percentage pricing accessible through $200 monthly recurring deposits.

Versus M1, Betterment falls short on fractional stock customization for self-directed investors. M1 allows you to build custom Pies containing specific stocks and ETFs chosen from over 6,000 securities with fractional shares built to exact percentages. Betterment selects the underlying funds in its core automated portfolios, and embedded ETF fees apply to those holdings. 

Worked cost example: On a $50,000 balance, Betterment charges 0.25% annually, which totals $125.00 per year ($50,000 multiplied by 0.0025). On M1, a $50,000 balance exceeds the $10,000 waiver threshold, resulting in a $0 platform fee. On an account balance of $5,000 without recurring deposits, Betterment charges $5 per month, or $60.00 per year. M1 charges $3 per month on that $5,000 balance, which equals $36.00 per year. For an investor with $100,000 in Betterment Premium, the 0.65% fee equals $650.00 annually.

alternatives.heading: Wealthfront
alternatives.body:
Wealthfront provides automated portfolio management and self-directed trading through two separate account structures. The Wealthfront Portfolio charges a flat annual advisory fee of 0.25%, with Wealthfront publishing an example showing that a $15,000 balance costs $3.18 per month. The Wealthfront Brokerage Account charges no advisory or management fees and requires $1 to get started, allowing clients to buy stocks and ETFs directly. For cash management, the Wealthfront Cash Account offers a 3.55% base APY with zero account fees, free 24/7 instant withdrawals, and reimbursement for two out-of-network automated teller machine (ATM) fees per month up to $7.50 each. Eligible new clients can receive an APY boost of 0.65% for three months on balances up to $150,000, bringing the rate to 4.45%.

Wealthfront fits investors who want automated portfolio management or a standalone commission-free brokerage account paired with high-yield cash.

Versus M1, Wealthfront does not provide M1's Pie-based system for self-directed stock pickers. While Wealthfront offers a fee-free Brokerage Account for individual stocks and ETFs, it does not structure portfolios into custom percentage Pies built with fractional shares. Wealthfront also does not list native margin borrowing on its self-directed accounts at a published rate comparable to M1's 5.90%.

Worked cost example: On a $20,000 automated portfolio, Wealthfront charges 0.25% annually, which equals $50.00 per year ($20,000 multiplied by 0.0025). On M1, a self-directed $20,000 account pays $0 in platform fees because the balance exceeds $10,000. On a balance of $10,000 or less, M1 charges its $3 monthly platform fee, which totals $36.00 over twelve months.

alternatives.heading: Fidelity
alternatives.body:
Fidelity provides self-directed brokerage accounts with $0 online commissions for US stocks, ETFs and options trades, although option contract fees apply. Fidelity enforces no account minimums to open an account. For automated management, Fidelity offers Fidelity Go, which requires no minimum to open and begins investing once an account reaches $10. Fidelity Go charges a $0 annual advisory fee for account balances under $25,000. Once an account balance reaches $25,000 or more, Fidelity Go charges an annual advisory fee of 0.35%, which includes one-on-one coaching calls and tax-loss harvesting on taxable accounts. Fidelity lists a margin base rate of 10.825%, with tiered effective rates including 12.075% on debit balances from $0 to $24,999.

Fidelity fits investors who want full brokerage services with zero account fees and a robo-advisor that is free for balances under $25,000.

Versus M1, Fidelity falls short on built-in margin borrowing costs. Fidelity charges an effective margin rate of 12.075% on balances up to $24,999, compared with M1's published margin rate of 5.90% for accounts holding at least $2,000 in eligible securities. Fidelity also lacks M1's Pie allocation model that lets users build to exact percentages using fractional shares.

Worked cost example: On a $30,000 balance in Fidelity Go, the 0.35% advisory fee equals $105.00 per year ($30,000 multiplied by 0.0035). On M1, a $30,000 self-directed portfolio incurs $0 in platform fees. If an investor borrows $5,000 on margin for one year, M1's 5.90% rate costs $295.00 in interest, whereas Fidelity lists a higher effective rate of 12.075% on balances up to $24,999.

alternatives.heading: Robinhood
alternatives.body:
Robinhood provides commission-free trading for US stocks, ETFs, options, cryptocurrency, futures and prediction markets, allowing investors to open an account with as little as $1. Robinhood offers an optional Gold subscription for $5 per month ($60 per year), with the first 30 days free. Robinhood Gold includes a 3.6% APY on eligible uninvested brokerage cash, instant deposits up to three times portfolio value, zero management fees on balances over $100,000 in Robinhood Strategies managed portfolios, and a 3% match on new Individual Retirement Account (IRA) contributions (up to $225 based on the 2026 limit, requiring one year on Gold and maintaining IRA assets for five years). Instant withdrawals incur a 1.5% fee.

Robinhood fits self-directed investors and active traders who want multi-asset trading and a 3% IRA contribution match through Gold.

Versus M1, Robinhood does not offer custom Pies built to exact percentages. Robinhood also charges $5 per month for Gold to unlock its 3.6% cash rate and IRA match, whereas M1 High-Yield Cash Account requires no monthly fee for balances over $10,000 and M1 Advisor is free for all M1 clients.

Worked cost example: A subscriber on Robinhood Gold pays $5 per month, which totals $60.00 per year. If that investor holds $10,000 or more in an M1 self-directed account, the M1 platform fee is $0. If an investor with a $5,000 balance holds uninvested cash in M1's High-Yield Cash Account at 3.35% APY, the simple one-year annual earnings equal $167.50 ($5,000 multiplied by 0.0335). Robinhood Gold offers a 3.6% APY on eligible brokerage cash alongside its $60.00 annual subscription cost.

alternatives.heading: Public
alternatives.body:
Public is an investing platform offering commission-free trading for US stocks, ETFs and Application Programming Interface (API) orders. Its High-Yield Cash Account lists a 3.30% APY on its cash page, alongside a 3.75% APY in promotional material. Public provides a Treasuries ladder yielding 4.41%, a Bond Account with an advertised 6.40% yield, an uncapped 1% match on IRA contributions and account transfers, and direct indexing starting at a $1,000 minimum across more than 100 customizable indices. Public also provides Crypto IRAs and an Options Rebate Program paying enrolled users $0.06 to $0.18 per stock or ETF options contract. Margin borrowing features a base rate of 5.15%, stepping down to a lowest listed rate of 4.20%. Securities accounts are protected by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) up to $500,000.

Public fits self-directed investors who want direct indexing across diverse indices, competitive cash yields without a subscription, and low margin borrowing rates.

Versus M1, Public does not feature M1's native Pie design where fractional shares build to exact percentages. While Public offers direct indexing from $1,000, M1 allows users to assemble stocks and ETFs into personal Pies with customized percentage allocations for any deposit size. 

Worked cost example: If an investor borrows $5,000 on margin for twelve months, Public's base margin rate of 5.15% costs $257.50 per year ($5,000 multiplied by 0.0515). On M1, borrowing $5,000 at its published 5.90% margin rate costs $295.00 per year ($5,000 multiplied by 0.059), making Public $37.50 cheaper in annual borrowing interest. On uninvested cash, M1 pays 3.35% APY (yielding $167.50 per year on $5,000), compared to Public's 3.30% base cash APY.

alternatives.heading: Acorns
alternatives.body:
Acorns provides automated micro-investing through three monthly subscription tiers: Bronze at $4 per month ($48 annually), Silver at $8 per month ($96 annually), and Gold at $12 per month ($144 annually). Acorns automatically rounds up spare change from linked card purchases and invests the difference into expert-built, diversified portfolios. Bronze includes investing, Round-Ups, and the Acorns Later retirement account. Silver adds an Emergency Savings account paying 3.59% APY, while Bronze includes a 1% IRA match. Gold includes a 3% match on new IRA contributions in the first year (up to $225 on a max contribution), and the Premium subscription includes $10,000 life insurance. Acorns Checking offers zero overdraft fees and access to 55,000 or more fee-free ATMs.

Acorns fits beginner investors who want to save spare change automatically into pre-built diversified portfolios without managing individual stock positions.

Versus M1, Acorns does not permit self-directed stock picking or custom allocation modeling. Acorns places funds into expert-built portfolios, whereas M1 allows users to choose from over 6,000 US-listed stocks and ETFs to construct custom Pies. Acorns also does not offer margin borrowing, and its monthly subscription fees apply regardless of balance size.

Worked cost example: An investor on Acorns Bronze pays $4 per month, totaling $48.00 per year. On Acorns Silver, the cost is $96.00 per year ($8 multiplied by 12), and on Acorns Gold, the cost is $144.00 per year ($12 multiplied by 12). On an account balance of $5,000, M1 charges $3 per month, which equals $36.00 annually, saving $12.00 compared to Acorns Bronze. Once an account exceeds $10,000, M1 charges $0 in platform fees, whereas Acorns continues charging $48 to $144 annually.

alternatives.heading: Webull
alternatives.body:
Webull provides self-directed trading with $0 commissions on US-listed stocks, ETFs and equity options. Certain index options incur a $0.50 per contract fee, and regulatory pass-through fees apply. Webull enforces no deposit minimums to open or maintain an account. Webull states that it generates revenue through stock loans, interest on credit balances, margin interest, and payment for order flow. For investors wanting advisory management, Webull offers managed accounts through Webull Advisors, an investment adviser registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Accounts carry SIPC protection up to $500,000, including $250,000 for cash claims. Webull charges an outgoing stock transfer fee of $75.

Webull fits active traders and options investors who require commission-free stock and options trading without deposit minimums.

Versus M1, Webull does not provide a Pie portfolio system for long-term investing. M1 allows investors to build to exact percentages using fractional shares. However, Webull permits continuous trading throughout market hours, which M1 does not support due to its scheduled batch trade windows.

Worked cost example: A self-directed investor maintaining a $5,000 balance on Webull pays $0 in ongoing platform fees. On M1, a $5,000 balance incurs the $3 monthly platform fee, which totals $36.00 over twelve months. Once the account balance exceeds $10,000, both Webull and M1 charge $0 in maintenance fees. If an investor transfers their portfolio out of Webull, Webull applies a $75.00 outgoing stock transfer fee.

stillBetterFit.heading: When M1 Is Still the Better Fit
stillBetterFit.body:
M1 remains the closer match for long-term investors who want to build a custom portfolio of individual stocks and ETFs using fractional shares. M1's signature Pie structure lets you select from over 6,000 US-listed securities and assign target percentages to each slice. Self-directed brokerage accounts carry no commission, trading or management fees. M1 Advisor acts as a free fiduciary AI financial advisor to assist with portfolio design and questions. In addition to individual taxable accounts, M1 supports joint accounts, custodial accounts, trusts, Traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, Simplified Employee Pension (SEP) IRAs and cryptocurrency via Bakkt.

For borrowing, M1 integrates margin loans at a published 5.90% interest rate directly into brokerage accounts holding at least $2,000 in eligible securities. Fidelity lists a 12.075% effective rate on debit balances under $25,000. For cash reserves, the M1 High-Yield Cash Account pays 3.35% APY on uninvested cash with a $100 initial deposit requirement, and sweeps deposits to partner banks to provide Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) coverage up to an aggregate of $4.75 million. Automated Customer Account Transfer (ACAT) incoming transfers take 4 to 7 business days with no incoming transfer fee, and 401(k), 403(b) or 457 retirement rollovers into an M1 IRA carry no incoming fee and typically finish within two to three weeks. Brokerage services are provided by M1 Finance LLC, a member of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) and SIPC, protecting securities up to $500,000 (including $250,000 for cash).

Who This Is Not For:

- Active day traders who need real-time limit orders, extended-hours trading, or continuous order execution throughout the day, because M1 executes trades only once or twice daily in batch windows.
- Options, futures, mutual fund, or OTC stock investors, because M1 does not offer these asset classes.
- Short sellers, as M1 does not support short positions.
- Investors with under $10,000 who want to avoid monthly fees entirely, because M1 charges a $3 monthly platform fee on balances of $10,000 or less.
- Hands-off investors who want a robo-advisor to pick and maintain their entire stock allocation without personal input; Betterment and Wealthfront provide automated management instead.

What Would Change Our Answer:

- M1 altering its $3 monthly platform fee or lowering the $10,000 threshold required to waive it.
- M1 adjusting its published 5.90% margin borrowing interest rate or changing the $2,000 minimum portfolio requirement.
- Betterment eliminating its $5 monthly charge on balances under $24,000 that lack recurring deposits.
- Fidelity Go modifying its $25,000 threshold for free advisory management.
- Robinhood Gold altering its $5 monthly subscription price or its 3% IRA contribution match terms.
- Public changing its 5.15% base margin borrowing rate or its cash account yield.

verdict: M1 provides fractional-share Pie investing, a 5.90% margin rate and 3.35% cash APY, with its $3 monthly fee waived on balances over $10,000. Betterment and Wealthfront fit investors wanting automated robo-portfolios managed at a 0.25% fee. Fidelity provides full commission-free brokerage alongside Fidelity Go at $0 under $25,000, Public provides direct indexing and lower margin rates, Robinhood delivers multi-asset trading with an IRA match on Gold, Acorns automates spare-change roundups, and Webull offers commission-free trading without minimums. Compare your portfolio balance against the $10,000 waiver threshold and calculate your margin borrowing needs before opening an account.

faqs.question: Does M1 Finance charge fees?
faqs.answer: M1 charges no commission, trading or management fees for self-directed brokerage accounts. It charges a platform fee of $3 per month, which is waived for clients with more than $10,000 across the platform. M1 Advisor is free for all M1 clients. Other regulatory and account closure fees may apply as disclosed on M1's fee schedule.

faqs.question: Is M1 a bank?
faqs.answer: No. M1 is not a bank. Brokerage services are provided by M1 Finance LLC, a member of FINRA and SIPC. Cash in the M1 High-Yield Cash Account is swept to partner banks, making it eligible for FDIC insurance up to an aggregate of $4.75 million.

faqs.question: Can I place limit orders at M1?
faqs.answer: No. M1 does not support limit orders, day trading or extended-hours trading. Orders execute during scheduled trade windows that run once or twice per day, designed for long-term investing rather than real-time trading.

faqs.question: Which M1 alternative has a subscription?
faqs.answer: Robinhood offers an optional Gold subscription for $5 per month ($60 per year) with a 3.6% cash APY and a 3% IRA contribution match. Acorns operates entirely on subscriptions: Bronze costs $4 per month, Silver costs $8 per month, and Gold costs $12 per month.

faqs.question: Which alternative lists a margin rate?
faqs.answer: Public lists a base margin borrowing rate of 5.15% (with lower rates down to 4.20%), while Fidelity lists a base rate of 10.825% with an effective rate of 12.075% on balances under $25,000. M1 lists a margin borrowing rate of 5.90% for accounts with at least $2,000 in eligible securities.

faqs.question: Which alternative picks the portfolio for you?
faqs.answer: Betterment and Wealthfront build automated portfolios for a 0.25% annual fee. Fidelity Go also selects and manages portfolios, charging $0 for balances under $25,000 and 0.35% for balances of $25,000 or more. Acorns allocates funds into expert-built portfolios under its monthly subscription tiers.
